subject: submarine crew
title: What If You Lived Underwater for Months? Submariners Lose 40% of a Vitamin

scenes.text: What if you lived underwater for months, no sunlight? Submariners do, and their bodies keep score.
The only daylight comes through a periscope. For decades, crews ran on an 18-hour day: about twelve hours working, six asleep.
Their body clocks never agreed. Saliva tests on a three-month patrol showed the internal rhythm stayed stuck near 24 hours.
After about 30 days, the fresh fruit and vegetables run out. Step counts drop by more than half.
And with no sun, vitamin D falls. In one study it dropped 40 percent by the end of a patrol, unless the crew took supplements.
The reactor can run for decades. What actually sends a submarine home is simpler: the crew runs out of food.

description:
What if you lived underwater for months? Submarine crews see daylight only through a periscope and for decades worked an 18-hour day, while their body clocks stayed near 24 hours.
Fresh food runs out after about 30 days, physical activity falls by more than half, and in a US Navy study vitamin D levels dropped about 40 percent over a patrol without supplements. A nuclear submarine's endurance is limited by food, not fuel.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: A 2015 study found that crews switched to a normal 24-hour schedule slept just as well on day 51 of a deployment as on day one. Could you handle three months without seeing the sky? And what should we run through next?
